BRICS backs Palestine
Haifa
ISRAEL

BRICS backs Palestine


• On 15 May 2026, BRICS foreign ministers met at Bharat
  Mandapam in New Delhi under India’s chairmanship.

• The meeting reaffirmed support for an independent and viable
  State of Palestine within the pre-1967 borders, with East
  Jerusalem as its capital.

• No joint statement was issued because members disagreed on the
  wider West Asia conflict; instead, a Chair’s Statement and
  Outcome Document was released.

BRICS backs Palestine


History of Palestine –

• For about 400 years, Palestine was part of the Ottoman Empire,
  with a majority Muslim Arab population.

• The region also had Christian Arabs and a small, centuries-old Jewish
  community living mostly in Jerusalem, Safed, Tiberias and Hebron.

• During World War I, Britain issued the Balfour Declaration
  (1917) , promising a “national home for the Jewish people” in
  Palestine while supposedly protecting the rights of non-Jewish
  communities.

BRICS backs Palestine


• After the war, the League of Nations granted Britain a Mandate
  over Palestine in 1922, giving it administrative control.

• Large-scale Jewish immigration, rising Arab nationalism and violent
  clashes between the two communities steadily undermined British
  rule.

• By the 1930s, Britain tried to restrict Jewish immigration, but the
  conflict only intensified, especially after the Holocaust.

BRICS backs Palestine


• In 1947, Britain announced it would end the Mandate and handed the
  problem to the United Nations.

• The UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 181,
  recommending the division of Palestine into a Jewish state and an
  Arab state, with Jerusalem placed under international control.

• Jewish leaders accepted the plan, but Arab leaders rejected it
  outright, refusing to recognise any Jewish state in Palestine.

BRICS backs Palestine


• When the British Mandate ended on 14 May 1948, Israel declared
  independence.

• Neighbouring Arab states (Egypt, Jordan, Syria, Iraq) attacked the
  new state, but Israel expanded its territory beyond the partition
  borders.

• About 750,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled from their
  homes – an event Palestinians call the Nakba (catastrophe).

BRICS backs Palestine


• In June 1967, Israel launched a pre-emptive strike against Egypt,
  Syria and Jordan – the Six-Day War.

• Israel captured the West Bank, Gaza Strip, East Jerusalem, the
  Golan Heights and the Sinai Peninsula, placing millions of
  Palestinians under military occupation.

• The pre-1967 borders (the Green Line) became the reference point
  for a future two-state solution.

BRICS backs Palestine


• The Palestine Liberation Organisation (PLO) was founded in
  1964, and in 1974 the Arab League recognised it as the “sole
  legitimate representative of the Palestinian people”.

• The First Intifada (1987–1993) was a mass uprising of civil
  disobedience, strikes and protests against the occupation.

• A much more violent Second Intifada (2000–2005) erupted,
  leading to thousands of deaths and a severe crackdown by the Israeli
  military.

BRICS backs Palestine


• The Oslo Accords were the first direct, face-to-face agreement
  between Israel and the PLO, signed in 1993 and 1995.

• They created the Palestinian Authority (PA) and gave it limited
  self-rule over parts of the West Bank and Gaza.

• However, the accords did not resolve core issues: borders, Jerusalem,
  refugees or Israeli settlements.

BRICS backs Palestine


• 2005: Israel unilaterally withdrew all its settlers and soldiers
  from the Gaza Strip, but retained control over its airspace, maritime
  border and most land crossings.

• 2006: Hamas won a landslide victory in Palestinian legislative
  elections. The West and Israel refused to accept the result.

• 2007: After fierce fighting, Hamas drove the PA from Gaza and
  established exclusive control there, splitting the Palestinian
  territories politically.

BRICS backs Palestine


• For years, Palestine sought full UN membership, but the US pledged
  to veto it in the Security Council.

• In 2012, the UN General Assembly upgraded Palestine to
  “non-member observer State” status by a large majority.

• This allowed Palestine to join international treaties and agencies
  (such as the ICC), though it is still not a full UN member.

BRICS backs Palestine


• In 2004, the ICJ issued an advisory opinion declaring Israel’s
  separation wall in the West Bank illegal and calling for its
  dismantlement.

• On 7 October 2023, Hamas launched a massive coordinated attack
  on Israel from Gaza, killing approximately 1,200 people (mostly
  civilians) and taking over 250 hostages to Gaza, including women,
  children and foreign nationals.

• In 2024, the ICJ ruled that Israel’s prolonged occupation of
  Palestinian territory is unlawful and demanded its end.

BRICS backs Palestine


• Article 1(2) of the UN Charter enshrines the principle
  of “self-determination of peoples” as a core purpose of the
  United Nations.

• The International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
  (ICCPR) and the International Covenant on Economic, Social
  and Cultural Rights (ICESCR) – both adopted in 1966 –
  guarantee the right to self-determination in their common Article 1.

• Palestine’s claim to statehood is rooted in this fundamental principle
  of self-determination of peoples.

BRICS backs Palestine


• UNSC Resolution 242, adopted unanimously on 22 November
  1967, called for the “withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from
  territories occupied” in the Six-Day War.

• It also affirmed the right of every state in the region “to live in peace
  within secure and recognised boundaries”.

• This resolution remains the cornerstone of the land-for-peace formula
  and is repeatedly cited in support of the pre-1967 borders.

BRICS backs Palestine


• The Arab Peace Initiative was adopted by the Arab League in
  2002 at its Beirut summit.

• It offers normalisation of relations between Arab countries and
  Israel in return for Israel’s full withdrawal from occupied territories,
  the creation of a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its
  capital, and a “just solution” to the refugee problem.

BRICS backs Palestine


• Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions prohibits violence
  against persons taking no active part in hostilities and applies to
  non-international armed conflicts.

• The Fourth Geneva Convention (1949) specifically protects
  civilians in occupied territories and prohibits the transferring of an
  occupying power’s own civilian population into the territory it
  occupies.

• The construction of Israeli settlements in the West Bank is widely
  regarded as a violation of the Fourth Geneva Convention.

BRICS backs Palestine


• The Quartet – composed of the UN, the US, the EU and Russia –
  was established in 2002 to mediate the Israel-Palestine peace
  process.

• It has promoted a road map for peace based on the two-state
  solution. BRICS ministers, while not speaking on behalf of the
  Quartet, aligned their statement with the Quartet’s long-standing
  principles.

• The two-state solution refers to the creation of two sovereign
  states – Israel and Palestine – living side by side in peace and
  security. It is the universally accepted framework for resolving
  the Israel-Palestine conflict.

BRICS backs Palestine


What is BRICS? –

• The term "BRIC" was coined in 2001 by economist Jim O'Neill of
  Goldman Sachs in a paper titled "The World Needs Better
  Economic BRICs," identifying Brazil, Russia, India, and China as
  rapidly growing economies.

• The four countries were labelled "whale countries" due to their
  immense territory, large populations, abundant resources and
  growing economic weight.

BRICS backs Palestine


• The formal grouping began in 2006: the economy ministers met in
  St. Petersburg in June.

• It followed by the first BRIC Foreign Ministers' meeting on the
  sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York in September.

• The first BRIC Summit was held in Yekaterinburg, Russia, on
  16 June 2009, where leaders discussed the global financial crisis
  and ways to strengthen the group.

BRICS backs Palestine


• South Africa joined the group in 2010, formally changing the
  acronym from BRIC to BRICS at the foreign ministers' meeting in
  New York in September 2010.

• The decision to add an African country kept the acronym intact and
  gave the bloc a strategic foothold on the African continent.

• South Africa attended its first BRICS Summit in Sanya, China, in
  2011, marking the official expansion of the bloc from four to five
  members.

BRICS backs Palestine


• At the 6th BRICS Summit in Fortaleza, Brazil, in 2014, the
  grouping established two of its most significant institutions:

     ➢ The New Development Bank (NDB)

     ➢ The Contingent Reserve Arrangement (CRA)

• The New Development Bank (NDB) officially began functioning
  in 2016, with its headquarters located in Shanghai, China. It has
  an African regional center in South Africa.

BRICS backs Palestine


• In January 2024, BRICS welcomed five new full members: Egypt,
  Ethiopia, Iran, and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and
  Saudi Arabia.

• In January 2025, Indonesia became the bloc’s tenth full
  member, marking a historic expansion and the dawn of the "Big
  BRICS" era.

• Following this, nine other countries were inducted as "partner
  countries" in 2025, including Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan,
  Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, and Uzbekistan.

BRICS backs Palestine


• The expanded BRICS now represents nearly half of the world’s
  population and contributes over 30 percent of global GDP,
  accounting for more than 50 percent of global economic growth.

• More than 30 countries have formally applied to join the bloc.

BRICS backs Palestine

India’s Chairmanship –

• India formally assumed the rotating BRICS chairmanship on 1
  January 2026, taking over from Russia, and will hold the position
  for the entire calendar year.

• This is the first time India chairs the expanded BRICS bloc that
  now includes Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran and the United Arab Emirates,
  making the grouping more diverse than ever.

• The official theme of India’s chairship is “Building for Resilience,
  Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability” , captured in the
  very acronym BRICS.

BRICS backs Palestine


• India’s Four Priority Pillars for the Chairmanship:

   ➢ Resilience - supply chains, markets, early-warning,
    climate-resilient infrastructure

   ➢ Innovation - digital public infrastructure, fintech, AI
    governance, startup platform, incubator network

   ➢ Cooperation - reformed multilateralism, partner-country model,
    trade, agriculture, health

   ➢ Sustainability - climate action, clean energy, green finance,
    Global South needs

BRICS backs Palestine


• Under India’s chairship, the BRICS Foreign Ministers’ Meeting
  was held at Bharat Mandapam, New Delhi on 14-15 May 2026,
  chaired by External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar.

• The meeting focused on three broad thematic sessions:

  ➢ Global and regional matters;

  ➢ Reform of global governance and the multilateral system; and

  ➢ “BRICS at 20”, reflecting on the grouping’s evolution over two
   decades.

BRICS backs Palestine


• India’s BRICS Sherpa is Sudhakar Dalela.

• The agenda covered five priority files: AI governance for
  development, reformed multilateralism, climate finance for the Global
  South, expansion and partner-country protocol, and the response to
  the West Asia situation.

• Ministers strongly endorsed comprehensive reform of the UN,
  including expansion of the Security Council.

BRICS backs Palestine


Recent News –

• BRICS called for an independent State of Palestine within the
  pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, and
  supported Palestine’s full membership in the UN.

• BRICS ministers endorsed the Arab Peace Initiative (2002) in
  their statement.

• The BRICS statement is a powerful endorsement of the two-state
  solution by the world’s major emerging economies.

BRICS backs Palestine


• Iran and the UAE had particularly sharp exchanges on the Gaza
  paragraph and on the situation in the Red Sea and the Strait of
  Hormuz.

• The draft paragraph referred to the Gaza Strip as an “inseparable
  part of the Occupied Palestinian Territory” and called for handing
  over Gaza’s control from Hamas to the Palestinian Authority.

• Iran’s Foreign Minister Araghchi asserted that the Strait of
  Hormuz falls entirely within the territorial waters of Iran and
  Oman, and therefore there are “no international waters in between”.

BRICS backs Palestine


• He said that the future arrangement for navigation through the strait
  must be managed between Iran and Oman alone.

• Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov assured India of continued
  energy supplies from Russia and discussed cooperation on
  the North-South Transport Corridor (NSTC), payment
  settlement in national currencies, and nuclear energy cooperation.

• The NSTC is a multi-modal route connecting India to Russia and
  Europe via Iran, and its viability depends on political stability in
  Iran.

BRICS backs Palestine


• External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar reiterated India’s support for
  a two-state solution where a sovereign Palestinian state lives side
  by side with Israel in peace and security.

• India has consistently backed the Palestinian cause while
  maintaining diplomatic relations with Israel.

• The New Delhi meeting gave India an opportunity to showcase
  its traditional support for Palestine on a global platform.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Government of India has notified the Viksit Bharat–
  Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) (VB-
  GRAMG) Act, 2025, which will come into force nationwide from 1
  July 2026, replacing the nearly 20-year-old MGNREGA scheme.

• The Act raises the statutory employment guarantee from 100 days
  to 125 days of wage employment per rural household per
  financial year.

• On 11 May 2026, the Ministry of Rural Development formally
  notified that the VB-GRAMG Act will be brought into force with effect
  from 1 July 2026 across all States and Union Territories.

VB-GRAMG Act
MGNREGA –

• Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was
  enacted in 2005 and came into force on 2 February 2006 as the
  world’s largest work guarantee programme.

• The Act was inspired by the Maharashtra Employment
  Guarantee Scheme (MEGS) of 1972, which itself originated as a
  drought relief programme in the early 1970s.

• The Act was structured to be demand-driven: employment was
  provided on demand, and funds were allocated accordingly.

VB-GRAMG Act



• Although the Constitution does not expressly recognise the right to
  work as a fundamental right, Article 41 (Directive Principles)
  directs the State to make effective provision for securing the right to
  work.

• The Supreme Court, in Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal
  Corporation (1985) , recognised that the right to livelihood is an
  integral facet of the right to life under Article 21.

VB-GRAMG Act


• MGNREGA guaranteed 100 days of wage employment per
  household per year, with the wage rate linked to the Consumer
  Price Index for Agricultural Labour (CPI-AL).

• The Act provided for an unemployment allowance – if a person
  seeking work was not provided employment within 15 days, the
  state government was required to pay unemployment allowance for
  each day of delay.

• The wage-material ratio mandated that at least 60% of total
  expenditure should be on wages, with material costs limited to
  40%, and contractors were prohibited from executing works under
  the scheme.

VB-GRAMG Act


• Under MGNREGA, the Central Government undertook 100% of the
  wage costs (which constitute the bulk of the expenditure) while
  states contributed 25% of material costs.

• This funding pattern effectively made the Central Government the
  primary financial guarantor of the right to employment, relieving
  states from an open-ended financial burden.

• When states submitted annual work plans based on demand, the
  Centre was obligated to release funds accordingly.

VB-GRAMG Act
Features of New Act –

• With effect from 1 July 2026, the MGNREGA will stand repealed,
  along with all rules, notifications and guidelines issued under it.

• However, existing e-KYC-verified MGNREGA job cards will
  remain valid until new “Gramin Rozgar Guarantee Cards” are
  issued, ensuring a smooth administrative transition.

• Workers with pending e-KYC verification will not be denied
  employment, and fresh registrations will continue at the gram
  panchayat level.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Act provides a statutory guarantee of not less than 125
  days of wage employment per rural household in each financial year
  (Section 5(1)), an increase of 25 days over MGNREGA.

• This period is to be provided during the period outside the
  agricultural pause.

• The guaranteed employment is to be provided to households whose
  adult members volunteer to undertake unskilled manual work,
  with the work linked to durable asset creation.

VB-GRAMG Act


• State governments are empowered to notify an aggregated pause
  period up to 60 days in a financial year during which works under
  the scheme will not be undertaken (Section 6).

• This pause is intended to cover peak agricultural seasons,
  including sowing and harvesting, to facilitate adequate availability of
  agricultural labor.

• The 60-day pause provision has been criticised as
  effectively reducing the effective work guarantee to 65 days,
  because the provision does not require states to compensate for lost
  work days during the pause.

VB-GRAMG Act


• Wages must be paid on a weekly basis or, in any case, within 15
  days of completion of work.

• In case of delay beyond the stipulated period, delay
  compensation shall be payable in accordance with Schedule II of
  the Act, reinforcing wage security and protecting workers from
  delays.

• The unemployment allowance provision (payable if work is not
  provided within 15 days of demand) has been retained from
  MGNREGA, with rates linked to the notified wage rate.

VB-GRAMG Act


• Unlike MGNREGA (where the Centre undertook all wage costs), VB-
  GRAMG will be implemented as a Centrally Sponsored
  Scheme with shared financing between Centre and States.

• The fund-sharing pattern will be 60:40 for all states (Centre 60%,
  State 40%), and 90:10 for North-eastern and Himalayan
  States (Union Territories without legislatures will receive full central
  funding).

• The State Government will continue to pay unemployment
  allowance and compensation, and will also bear any expenditure
  incurred in excess of the normative allocation.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Act empowers the Central Government to determine state-wise
  normative allocation for each financial year – a fixed spending
  ceiling.

• Any expenditure incurred by a State in excess of this allocation
  must be borne by the State government itself, converting the
  earlier “open-ended” demand-driven scheme into a budget-capped
  program.

• The parameters for fixing these allocations will be prescribed by the
  Central Government later through Rules.

VB-GRAMG Act

• Wage employment under the Act is explicitly aligned with the creation
  of durable public assets across four priority thematic
  domains (Schedule I):

 ➢ Water security and water-related works (irrigation,
   conservation, ponds)；

 ➢ Core rural infrastructure (roads, bridges, culverts)；

 ➢ Livelihood-related infrastructure (rural haats, storage
   structures, work sheds, livestock shelters)； and

 ➢ Works to mitigate extreme weather events (flood control, soil
   conservation).

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Act makes at least one-third participation of
  women mandatory, with special focus on women-headed
  households (through special job cards) and on single women.

• Crèche facilities are to be provided at worksites where five or more
  children under five years accompany working women, and a woman
  worker is to be appointed to care for them.

• One-third representation of women is mandatory in the
  Central Rojgar Guarantee Council and State Rojgar
  Guarantee Councils to be constituted under the Act.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The VB-GRAMG Bill was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 16
  December 2025, passed by the Lok Sabha on 18 December, and
  cleared by the Rajya Sabha after midnight on 19 December 2025.

• The Bill received Presidential assent on 21 December 2025,
  with the Act taking effect six months later.

• The entire legislative process was completed in just six days – a
  speed that drew criticism from Opposition leaders, including Punjab
  Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann, who accused the Centre of “rushing
  the law through Parliament within 14 hours”.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The total annual outlay for the scheme is estimated at
  approximately ₹1.51 lakh crore (including State shares), with the
  Centre’s share projected at ₹95,692 crore.

• This represents the highest Budget Estimate allocation ever made
  for a rural employment programme in India – 40% of the total
  budget of the Department of Rural Development.

• For 2026-27, the Department of Rural Development’s budget is ₹2.2
  lakh crore.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The Act retains provisions for biometric authentication for
  transactions, geospatial technology for planning and
  monitoring, and mobile application-based dashboards for real-time
  tracking.

• Section 20 of the Act reinforces social audits conducted by
  Gram Sabhas, ensuring community oversight, transparency and
  inclusion.

• However, civil society groups like LibTech India have argued that
  the Act has no new provisions to mitigate corruption and that
  technology should not become the “sole gateway to employment,
  wages, or accountability”.

VB-GRAMG Act


• The new VB-GRAMG Act removes the mandatory universalization
  clause that was present in MGNREGA (which required the Act to be
  extended to the whole of rural India within five years).

• Under Section 5(1) of the VB-GRAMG Act, employment shall be
  provided only “in such rural areas in the State as may be
  notified by the Central Government”.

• Critics argue that this shift empowers the Central Government
  to indefinitely exclude some rural areas from the employment
  guarantee, fundamentally altering the character of the right to work.

VB-GRAMG Act


• In December 2025, the Punjab Assembly unanimously passed a
  resolution against the Centre’s move to replace MGNREGA.

• The resolution argued that VB-GRAMG converts a demand-driven
  scheme into a norm-based scheme tied to centrally-determined
  budgets instead of labour demand, potentially converting the
  “guarantee” into a budget-capped provision.

• Union Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan, however, termed the special
  session of the Punjab Assembly “against the federal spirit of our
  Constitution” because a state legislature cannot reject a law passed
  by Parliament.
